title: Lifecycle & Propagation
purpose: Expand Lifecycle & Propagation from a five-section overview into a stage-based cultivation-science curriculum while preserving the existing V3 topic owner and V4 evidence-first guided-study layer.
learningOutcome: A learner should be able to follow a cannabis plant from a traceable seed lot or cutting through germination, establishment, clonal rooting, transplanting, vegetative development, reproductive transition, flowering, maturation and cycle completion; define stage transitions with observable biological criteria; distinguish germination from emergence and establishment; recognize major propagation failure points; and keep records that separate developmental change from environmental or management problems.
visualTargets: seed and embryo anatomy with germination sequence
radicle emergence versus emergence versus establishment
cloning workflow from donor to rooted cutting
adventitious root initiation on a cutting
lifecycle traceability record from lot or mother to final outcome

chapters.title: Seed Identity, Quality & Storage
chapters.objective: Start the lifecycle with traceable biological material and learn why supplied identity, viability, vigor, maturity and storage history are separate pieces of evidence.

lessons.title: The cannabis seed unit: achene, embryo and reserves
lessons.summary: Treat the commercial cannabis seed as a fruit-seed unit containing protective outer tissues, an embryo and stored reserves prepared to support early development before the seedling becomes fully photosynthetic.
lessons.cultivation: Understanding the seed as a living developmental package explains why early germination depends first on seed condition, water, oxygen and temperature rather than on external fertilizer.
lessons.observe: Record lot identity, physical damage, contamination, obvious immaturity and storage history, but do not infer viability from coat color, size or hardness alone.

lessons.title: Seed-lot identity and chain of custody
lessons.summary: Separate a supplied cultivar or strain name from a traceable lot record that preserves source, generation, parentage claim, receipt history, subdivisions, tests and planting events.
lessons.cultivation: A germination result or later phenotype is useful only when it can be connected reliably to the material that produced it.
lessons.observe: Keep same-named lots separate unless evidence supports combining them, and retain parent-lot identity whenever a package is subdivided.

lessons.title: Viability, vigor and lot uniformity
lessons.summary: Distinguish the ability to produce a normal seedling from the speed, uniformity and resilience with which a seed lot establishes.
lessons.cultivation: Two lots can reach the same final germination percentage while differing greatly in speed, uniformity and seedling quality, which changes planting and population planning.
lessons.observe: Track time to germination and final seedling categories instead of reducing lot quality to a single final percentage.

lessons.title: Storage, aging and dormancy questions
lessons.summary: Connect seed moisture, temperature stability, packaging, age and physiological state with deterioration while distinguishing true dormancy from nonviability or unsuitable test conditions.
lessons.cultivation: Stable dry and cool storage protects reserve material better than relying on age labels or refrigeration alone, and periodic retesting is more defensible than assuming an expiration date.
lessons.observe: When a lot performs poorly, verify storage and test conditions before labeling the seed dormant, dead or genetically weak.

knowledgeChecks: Why is a supplied strain name not a complete seed-lot identity?
How can a lot be viable yet have weak vigor?
Why does cool storage not compensate for excessive seed moisture?
What evidence is needed before calling an ungerminated seed dormant?

chapters.title: Germination: From Imbibition to Radicle Emergence
chapters.objective: Understand germination as a measurable biological sequence driven by hydration, metabolic restart, reserve use, temperature and oxygen rather than as a single yes-or-no event.

lessons.title: Imbibition and metabolic restart
lessons.summary: Follow the dry unit through rapid water uptake, membrane reorganization, repair and renewed metabolism before visible root emergence.
lessons.cultivation: Multiple germination methods can work when they provide repeatable water contact without drowning the seed; the biology matters more than the container or substrate fashion.
lessons.observe: Swelling alone does not prove viability, so continue tracking the seed through radicle emergence and subsequent normal development.

lessons.title: Reserve mobilization before photosynthetic independence
lessons.summary: Learn how stored lipids, proteins and carbohydrates support respiration, cell expansion and early root and shoot growth before the emerging seedling can meet most of its carbon demand through photosynthesis.
lessons.cultivation: External fertilizer does not power the earliest germination process and can add unnecessary salinity before a functional root system is established.
lessons.observe: When germination is slow, inspect seed condition, temperature, oxygen and moisture before reaching for additives or stimulants.

lessons.title: Temperature, moisture and oxygen as one system
lessons.summary: Treat germination temperature, water availability and gas exchange as interacting variables because saturated or compacted media can contain abundant water while restricting oxygen.
lessons.cultivation: The goal is moist and aerated, not flooded and not repeatedly dried. Seed-zone temperature should be measured where the seed actually sits rather than inferred from room temperature.
lessons.observe: Record seed-level temperature, watering method, drainage, media condition, odor and visible contamination when comparing germination outcomes.

lessons.title: Define the germination endpoint
lessons.summary: Use radicle protrusion as a defined germination event while keeping later emergence and normal seedling establishment as separate acceptance gates.
lessons.cultivation: Separating germinated, emerged and established reveals whether losses occur before root emergence, during mechanical emergence or after the seedling enters its new environment.
lessons.observe: Record newly germinated units by time and preserve each seed's lot identity when it is transferred or direct-sown.

knowledgeChecks: Why can a dead seed swell during imbibition?
What is the biological problem with a saturated germination medium?
Why should room temperature not automatically be treated as seed temperature?
How do germination, emergence and establishment differ?

chapters.title: Seedling Establishment
chapters.objective: Follow the plant from cotyledon opening through true-leaf development and early root expansion using developmental criteria rather than arbitrary calendar age.

lessons.title: Cotyledons, hypocotyl and first true leaves
lessons.summary: Recognize the structural transition from an emerged seedling supported partly by seed reserves to a young plant building new photosynthetic leaf area and an expanding root system.
lessons.cultivation: Stage labels should follow actual development because two seedlings of the same age can differ substantially in leaf, root and stem maturity.
lessons.observe: Record cotyledon opening, true-leaf appearance, node development and root progress rather than age alone.

lessons.title: Root-shoot balance during establishment
lessons.summary: Connect expansion of new roots with leaf area, transpiration demand and the seedling's increasing dependence on a functional root zone.
lessons.cultivation: A rapidly expanding shoot supported by a small or impaired root system has less hydraulic margin when light, heat or vapor demand increases.
lessons.observe: Pair shoot growth with root-zone moisture, root appearance and recovery between irrigation events.

lessons.title: Light, morphology and early stretch
lessons.summary: Understand how light quantity, direction and competition interact with genetics and temperature to influence seedling elongation and leaf development.
lessons.cultivation: Excessive elongation is a morphology observation, not a diagnosis by itself; light, temperature, density and genetics all belong in the comparison.
lessons.observe: Measure internode length, stem diameter, leaf expansion and plant-to-plant uniformity instead of relying on a vague stretched/not-stretched label.

lessons.title: Seedling release criteria and failure patterns
lessons.summary: Define when a seedling is established enough for the next stage and distinguish damping-off, mechanical injury, water stress, salinity and poor root-zone aeration as different failure pathways.
lessons.cultivation: A release gate based on active roots, healthy new growth and stable water balance is more transferable than a rule such as move every plant on day seven.
lessons.observe: Track lesion location, stem integrity, root color, media moisture, temperature and disease spread before assigning a cause to seedling collapse.

knowledgeChecks: Why is seedling age alone a weak transplant or release criterion?
How does increasing leaf area change hydraulic demand on the root system?
What measurements improve an assessment of early stretch?
Which observations help separate damping-off from simple water stress?

chapters.title: Clonal Propagation & Mother Stock
chapters.objective: Understand a cutting as wounded shoot tissue that must survive water imbalance, initiate adventitious roots and retain traceable identity while sanitation limits pathogen transfer.

lessons.title: Mother-stock selection and donor condition
lessons.summary: Treat donor identity, developmental state, health, recent stress, pest and disease status and cutting position as part of the propagation input rather than assuming every shoot is equivalent.
lessons.cultivation: Cloning preserves genotype but does not freeze physiological condition or erase pests and pathogens carried with the cutting.
lessons.observe: Record donor ID, source node or shoot position, recent treatments, visible health and date before the cutting is separated.

lessons.title: Wounding, water balance and cutting preparation
lessons.summary: Explain why a severed shoot immediately loses root-supplied water and must control transpiration while the wound seals and rooting processes begin.
lessons.cultivation: Humidity and light management should reduce water-loss pressure without creating stagnant, persistently wet conditions that favor tissue decline or disease.
lessons.observe: Track turgor, leaf condition, stem base appearance, media moisture and recovery pattern rather than judging rooting from leaf appearance alone.

lessons.title: Adventitious root initiation
lessons.summary: Follow the developmental shift in which competent stem tissues form root initials and new roots under coordinated hormonal, carbohydrate and environmental signals.
lessons.cultivation: Rooting products cannot compensate for unsuitable donor tissue, poor sanitation, water imbalance or an oxygen-limited propagation medium.
lessons.observe: Use actual root emergence and continued root extension as the rooting endpoint rather than a fixed number of days.

lessons.title: Rooted-clone acclimation and release
lessons.summary: Transition newly rooted cuttings from a protected high-humidity propagation environment toward the light, airflow and evaporative conditions of normal vegetative growth.
lessons.cultivation: Abrupt environmental change can exceed the new root system's ability to support the shoot even when roots are visible.
lessons.observe: Release clones when new roots are actively extending, the shoot maintains turgor under progressively normal conditions and new growth is healthy.

knowledgeChecks: What does cloning preserve, and what biological conditions can still change or transfer?
Why is water balance difficult immediately after a cutting is taken?
Why is visible root emergence better than calendar age as a rooting endpoint?
What evidence shows that a rooted clone is ready to leave propagation conditions?

chapters.title: Transplanting, Acclimation & Early Vegetative Growth
chapters.objective: Connect container geometry, root occupation, media condition and environmental change with the transition from propagation into stable vegetative growth.

lessons.title: Container occupancy and transplant timing
lessons.summary: Use root distribution, media behavior, plant water demand and available volume together to decide when a plant is outgrowing its current root environment.
lessons.cultivation: Transplanting too early wastes root-zone volume and can complicate moisture control; waiting too long can produce uneven moisture, restriction and circling roots.
lessons.observe: Inspect root distribution and irrigation behavior rather than using canopy width or plant age as the only transplant trigger.

lessons.title: Root disturbance and transplant shock
lessons.summary: Understand transplant shock as a temporary imbalance that can result from root injury, changed moisture distribution, new chemistry, temperature change or altered evaporative demand.
lessons.cultivation: The goal is to minimize simultaneous stressors rather than to assume every transplant requires a stimulant or corrective feeding.
lessons.observe: Record root disturbance, media condition, irrigation, temperature, light and recovery of new growth after the move.

lessons.title: Hardening and environmental acclimation
lessons.summary: Treat hardening as gradual physiological adjustment to a new light, temperature, humidity, airflow or outdoor environment rather than as a single move event.
lessons.cultivation: A plant adapted to protected propagation conditions may respond poorly to a sudden increase in radiation or evaporative demand despite having a healthy root system.
lessons.observe: Change one major exposure dimension at a time when possible and track turgor, leaf temperature, new growth and recovery.

lessons.title: Confirming vegetative establishment
lessons.summary: Define early vegetative establishment by sustained new root and shoot growth, stable irrigation response and expanding nodes rather than by survival alone.
lessons.cultivation: A plant that merely remains alive after transplant is not necessarily ready for aggressive training, environmental escalation or reproductive transition.
lessons.observe: Look for repeatable new growth and stable daily response before increasing management intensity.

knowledgeChecks: Why can irrigation behavior reveal container restriction before canopy appearance does?
What different mechanisms can produce the umbrella term transplant shock?
Why should acclimation be gradual after protected propagation?
What distinguishes survival from successful vegetative establishment?

chapters.title: Vegetative Development & Crop Readiness
chapters.objective: Track the expanding root-shoot system through node production, branching, leaf-area development and resource allocation until the plant is biologically ready for the next intended stage.

lessons.title: Nodes, branches and expanding architecture
lessons.summary: Follow vegetative development through repeated production of nodes, internodes, leaves and axillary shoots that build the future canopy.
lessons.cultivation: Node count, branch position and internode length provide more useful developmental information than height alone.
lessons.observe: Track architecture over time and compare new growth with earlier nodes to identify changes in growth pattern.

lessons.title: Source-sink growth and biomass allocation
lessons.summary: Understand that mature leaves supply carbon while roots, shoot tips and developing branches compete as sinks whose priorities shift with stage and environment.
lessons.cultivation: Removing, bending or shading tissue changes the source-sink system and can redirect subsequent growth rather than simply subtracting biomass.
lessons.observe: Assess recovery and new growth after training before assuming the intended canopy response occurred.

lessons.title: Training timing and recovery capacity
lessons.summary: Place low- and high-stress training inside developmental context by considering meristem activity, stem maturity, root support and time available for recovery.
lessons.cultivation: Training belongs after stable establishment and should be judged by recovery and architecture, while detailed technique belongs in the dedicated Training & Canopy section.
lessons.observe: Document the intervention, tissue condition, time to resumed growth and any localized transport or wound problems.

lessons.title: Readiness for reproductive transition
lessons.summary: Define transition readiness as a management decision based on plant health, root-zone stability, canopy structure, developmental maturity and available space rather than plant age alone.
lessons.cultivation: Moving an unstable crop into a new developmental and environmental regime makes later problems harder to interpret because multiple variables change at once.
lessons.observe: Record baseline plant size, node development, root-zone performance and health before changing the reproductive signal.

knowledgeChecks: Why is height alone a weak measure of vegetative development?
How can a training intervention change source-sink relationships?
What evidence should show recovery before another high-stress intervention?
Why is a pre-transition baseline valuable for later troubleshooting?

chapters.title: Reproductive Transition, Sex Expression & Flower Development
chapters.objective: Follow the plant through photoperiod perception, preflower expression, transition stretch and progressive reproductive development while separating genotype, developmental state and environmental influence.

lessons.title: Photoperiod perception and the dark period
lessons.summary: Understand reproductive transition as a plant signaling response to light-dark timing, interpreted through photoreceptor and circadian systems rather than as a simple switch located in the flower.
lessons.cultivation: Consistent timing matters because the plant integrates light-dark information across days; the dedicated Lighting section should hold detailed fixture and DLI management.
lessons.observe: Record actual timer schedule, interruptions and stage response rather than assuming the programmed schedule is what the plant experienced.

lessons.title: Photoperiod versus autoflower development
lessons.summary: Separate photoperiod-sensitive reproductive timing from genotypes with reduced dependence on day length while recognizing that environment still influences growth rate, stress and final morphology.
lessons.cultivation: Autoflower does not mean environment-independent, and photoperiod plants do not all transition at identical rates after a schedule change.
lessons.observe: Record genotype type, emergence date, node development and first reproductive signs rather than using one universal calendar.

lessons.title: Preflowers and sex expression
lessons.summary: Identify reproductive structures at nodes and distinguish normal male, female and mixed sex-expression observations from assumptions based on vegetative morphology.
lessons.cultivation: Early, repeated inspection protects breeding and seedless-flower goals, while sex-expression conclusions should be based on reproductive structures rather than plant shape.
lessons.observe: Inspect multiple nodes over time and photograph ambiguous structures before making irreversible crop decisions.

lessons.title: Transition stretch and progressive flower formation
lessons.summary: Follow the coordinated shift in internode growth, branching behavior, floral initiation and reproductive sink demand that occurs during early flowering.
lessons.cultivation: Early flowering is a changing developmental phase, so architecture, water demand and nutrient demand should be interpreted against the stage rather than treated as static vegetative behavior.
lessons.observe: Track stretch, node response, flower-site progression and environmental changes together to distinguish normal transition from new stress.

knowledgeChecks: Why is reproductive transition more than a timer switch?
What does autoflower not imply about environmental sensitivity?
Which structures should be used to determine sex expression?
Why can water and carbon demand change during transition stretch?

chapters.title: Maturation, Senescence & Lifecycle Records
chapters.objective: Finish the crop cycle by separating progressive reproductive maturation from stress-induced decline, documenting the endpoint and carrying traceable observations forward into the next cycle.

lessons.title: Flower maturation is a sequence, not a date
lessons.summary: Treat reproductive maturation as a progression of structural, physiological and chemical changes rather than a single calendar endpoint inherited from a label.
lessons.cultivation: Breeder timing estimates can guide planning but should not replace direct observation of the actual crop and its environmental history.
lessons.observe: Use repeated observations from consistent plant positions and avoid making maturity decisions from one photograph or one isolated cue.

lessons.title: Developmental senescence versus stress decline
lessons.summary: Understand senescence as regulated late-stage aging and nutrient remobilization while recognizing that root problems, disease, salinity, drought and other stresses can produce superficially similar yellowing or tissue loss.
lessons.cultivation: Calling every late-stage color change normal fade can hide a correctable problem, while treating all senescence as deficiency can provoke unnecessary intervention.
lessons.observe: Compare stage, symptom location, progression, root-zone data and environmental history before deciding whether decline is developmental or pathological.

lessons.title: Close the cycle with outcome records
lessons.summary: Link the final crop outcome back to seed lot or mother ID, dates of stage transitions, environment, irrigation, nutrition, interventions, health events and representative images.
lessons.cultivation: A complete record turns one crop into evidence that can improve the next instead of leaving only memory and a harvest date.
lessons.observe: Preserve deviations and failures as carefully as successful settings because they explain why otherwise similar cycles diverged.

lessons.title: Compare cycles and revise stage gates
lessons.summary: Use repeated crops to refine germination, establishment, transplant, training, transition and maturation criteria while keeping genotype, environment and management differences visible.
lessons.cultivation: The goal is not to force every plant onto one calendar; it is to improve the rules used to recognize biological readiness and risk in the actual system.
lessons.observe: Change stage targets only when the record shows a repeatable relationship between the revised criterion and a better downstream outcome.

knowledgeChecks: Why should a label-based flowering time not be treated as the sole maturity criterion?
What evidence helps separate senescence from stress-related decline?
Which records are necessary to connect a final outcome to its propagation source?
How can repeated cycles improve stage-gate decisions without creating a rigid calendar?
